spec_choices.why: The designer chose 4 and the source allows 3 to 5. 3 is the minimum because an auction needs rivals and the sack needs enough unknown cards to hide one's own. 5 is the maximum because the hand and reveal structure is built for 5, and with more seats one's own card would barely affect the sack.

spec_choices.what: Talk kept as a simultaneous poll with broadcast
spec_choices.why: The source specifies simultaneous non-binding messages. Players disagree about the sack, since each wants others to drop or to overbid, so bluffing about one's placed card gives the others something to reason about.

spec_choices.what: Cards encoded as text labels cat_<value>, rabbit and dog
spec_choices.why: The rabbit and dog are both worth 0 but behave differently, so a label is needed to count dogs.

spec_choices.what: Cat card values listed as separate parameters cat_value_1 to cat_value_7
spec_choices.why: Each parameter must be a single number.

spec_choices.what: Sack winner computed as one key: bid * 100000 - mice * 100 - seat offset from start_seat
spec_choices.why: This puts the source's three-level tie-break (bid, fewer mice, seat order from the start player) into a single arithmetic maximum.
Cat points can never reach plus or minus 500, so the total is compared first and cat points break ties. Exact ties share the win, which is the source's draw.

spec_choices.what: Stay/drop choices and bids are public once revealed
spec_choices.why: The source reveals bids together, and paying the fee or receiving the drop payment is visible. Who placed which card stays secret.

A thoughtful player infers others' cards from the public discard, the reveals and their own removed card. They bluff in talk and weigh the 1-mouse fee against the 2-mouse drop payment. They also use the fewer-mice tie-break and the dog rule when sizing a bid.

simplifications.what: The shuffle is done by drawing the sack cards at random into a new order
simplifications.why: The engine shuffles by random draws from a list.

simplifications.what: The bank of mice is not tracked
simplifications.why: It is unlimited, so only player mice change.

simplifications.what: A draw is represented as a shared win among the players tied at the top
simplifications.why: The engine has no separate draw outcome.

variation.original_summary: Felicity the Cat in the Sack is a 3-5 player bluffing auction. Each round every player secretly adds a card (cats of positive or negative value, a rabbit, dogs) to a 'sack', and players bid mice in a rising auction while the sack is revealed bit by bit. Players who pass take a mouse card as consolation, and final score is cat points plus leftover mice.

review.evidence: The original has no dominant policy, but its rising auction with escalating mouse-card consolations (2,3,4,6) is complex. The previous sealed-bid variation failed because STAY weakly dominated DROP. A losing stayer got 3 mice and a dropper got 2. Winning at price 1 beats DROP whenever the sack is worth 3 or more, and the average sack is worth about 12.9. So the stay/drop poll and the first reveal decided nothing.

Every hand holds the same cards, so the deal matters little. What decides the game is reading which cards rivals dumped, valuing a partly revealed sack, and pacing mice over the rounds. Shuffling the sack adds noise, but it falls on everyone.

A weak player can still score by dropping or buying cheap sacks. A strong player can keep improving by counting used cards from the face-up discards, timing the Dog, choosing when to dump the -8 and -5, and bidding with rivals' mice in mind.

Sack contents are partly hidden, and each player knows only their own contribution. Rivals' contributions must be inferred from what has been revealed, from cards already used, and from table talk. The value of a lone Dog depends on the hidden cats.
Sack value, the Dog removal, bids, payments and totals are all arithmetic.

The original's clockwise rising auction, with refunds, ordered consolation cards and a reveal on every pass, is a long chain of conditional steps. The previous sealed-bid variation fits the platform but left the 4-player reveal count ambiguous.

problems: P1: STAY weakly dominates DROP. A losing stayer earns 3 mice and a dropper earns 2, so staying never costs anything and the stay/drop poll is an empty step.
P2: Because everyone always stays, the first reveal and the talk before the stay/drop choice inform nothing.
P3: The reveal counts per player count were unclear, especially for 4 players.
P4: Without any cost to staying, bidding 1 every round is a cheap fallback that collects consolation income with no risk.

changes.what: Staying costs a non-refundable entry fee of 1 mouse, paid when STAY is chosen. Losing stayers receive no consolation. Droppers receive 2 mice.
changes.why: A losing stayer now ends the round 3 mice behind a dropper (-1 against +2). Staying only pays when the chance of winning a good sack at a good price justifies it. DROP is not dominant either: if everyone else drops, a lone stayer wins at price 1 and nets V-2 against 2, which is better whenever V > 4.

changes.what: The stay/drop decision comes after the first reveal and the talk, and the entry fee makes it a real gamble.
changes.why: The revealed cards and the rivals' claims now decide whether paying to enter is worth it.

changes.what: Exact reveal counts are stated for every player count. With 3 players: 1 card in the first reveal, 1 in the second, 1 hidden. With 4 players: 2, then 1, with 1 hidden. With 5 players: 2, then 1, with 2 hidden.
changes.why: Removes the ambiguity, and every player count keeps at least one hidden card at bidding time.

changes.what: A player needs at least 2 mice to stay (1 for the fee and at least 1 to bid). Otherwise they must drop.
changes.why: Keeps the fee-plus-bid rule consistent. Always-STAY-bid-1 now bleeds 1 mouse per lost round and ends far behind.

keeps: Every player feeds one card per round into a shared sack, so you build the sack your rivals may buy
Cats with positive and negative values, a worthless Rabbit, and a Dog that cancels the top cat only when it is alone
Gradual revealing of the sack before and during bidding
A choice between bidding for the sack and taking a safe mouse income
Final score of cat points plus remaining mice, so mice are both bidding power and points

recommendation.reason: The sealed-sack structure works. An entry fee and a zero consolation for losing stayers restore a genuine stay/drop gamble that is informed by the reveal and the talk.

variation.name: Cat in the Sack: Paid Entry
variation.summary: Players secretly feed cards into a shuffled sack, see part of it, talk, then decide whether to pay a mouse to enter a sealed-bid auction for it or take a safe 2 mice. They must infer the hidden cards and their rivals' intentions.
variation.rules:
SETUP
- Every player receives the same 9 cards: cats worth -8, -5, 3, 5, 8, 11 and 15, one Rabbit worth 0, and one Dog worth 0.
- One card is removed at random from each hand. Its owner is told which card it is. No one else is told.
- Each player starts with 15 mice and 0 cat points. The bank of mice is unlimited.
- Seats are numbered. Seat 1 is the start player in round 1.
- The game lasts 8 rounds, so every remaining card is played.

EACH ROUND
1. Start player. In round 1 it is Seat 1. In each later round it is the next seat in order. The start player matters only for breaking ties.
2. Fill the sack. All players at the same time secretly choose one card from their hand and place it in the sack. Placed cards never return.
3. Shuffle. The engine shuffles the sack into a random order.
4. First reveal. Cards are shown from the front of the shuffled order. With 3 players, 1 card is shown. With 4 or 5 players, 2 cards are shown. Revealed cards do not say who placed them.
5. Talk. Every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others' messages. All messages are then shown. Claims are not binding and may be lies.
6. Stay or drop. All players at the same time choose STAY or DROP. A player with fewer than 2 mice must DROP.
7. Entry and drop payment. Each player who chose STAY pays 1 mouse to the bank immediately. This fee is never refunded. Each player who chose DROP receives 2 mice from the bank and is out for this round.
8. Second reveal. The next card in the shuffled order is shown to everyone.
9. Sealed bid. Every player who chose STAY secretly bids a whole number of mice, from 1 up to their current mice (counted after paying the fee). All bids are revealed together.
10. Winner. The highest bidder wins the sack.
   - If two or more players tie for the highest bid, the tied player with fewer current mice wins.
   - If they are still tied, the tied player who comes first in seat order, counting from the start player, wins.
   - If nobody stayed, nobody wins and the sack is discarded.
   - If exactly one player stayed, that player wins and pays their bid.
11. Sack value. All remaining sack cards are revealed. The sack's value is the sum of the cats in it. The Rabbit and Dogs are worth 0.
   - If exactly one Dog is in the sack and the sack holds at least one cat, the cat with the highest value is removed before summing.
   - Two or more Dogs have no effect.
12. Payment. The winner pays their bid to the bank and adds the sack's value to their cat points. The value may be negative.
13. Losing stayers receive nothing. They have already paid their fee.
14. Discard. All sack cards are discarded face up, so everyone can count which cards have been used.
15. End check. After round 8 the game ends.

SCORING
Each player's total is their cat points plus their mice.
variation.objective: After round 8 the player with the highest total (cat points plus mice) wins. If totals are tied, the tied player with the most cat points wins. If that is also tied, the game is a draw among those players.
variation.expected_effect:
Staying is now a priced risk. A losing stayer falls 3 mice behind a dropper, so players stay only when the revealed cards, the counted discards and the talk suggest a sack worth more than about bid + 3. DROP is not dominant either: when the table drops, a lone stayer buys the sack for 1 mouse.

Simple-policy checks:
- Always DROP ends with 31 points and 0 cat points. It loses to any player who buys two decent sacks at a margin, since a sack of value 12 bought for 4 nets 7 against DROP's 2.
- Always STAY bidding 1 loses about 1 mouse per lost round and ends near 7 plus a few cheap sacks, so it loses to sensible play.
- Always STAY bidding everything wins round 1 at a loss of about 15 mice, then is stuck dropping, so it loses.
- Random play overpays and enters bad sacks, so it loses.

Talk earns its place because interests conflict. Each player wants rivals to enter bad sacks (where they themselves dumped the -8 or the Dog) and to drop out of good sacks. A player who believes 'I put in the 15, stay!' may pay a fee and a bid for a sack holding the speaker's -8, or a lone Dog that wipes out the 15. A follower can therefore lose, and talk tests reading and bluffing. Endgame: the face-up discards make the last rounds a counting puzzle rather than an unravelling, because there is no cooperation to betray. Seat order only breaks ties and rotates, and all hands are identical apart from one removed card, which shapes what you can dump rather than who wins.

balanced.evidence: The core decision table is STAY-and-bid-1 against DROP, for one player, given what the others do. Case 1: someone else bids 2 or more, so you lose. STAY earns +3 mice (step 13); DROP earns +2 mice (step 7). STAY is better by 1. Case 2: every other stayer bids 1 and you hold the fewest mice, so you win at price 1. STAY nets V-1, where V is the sack value; DROP nets +2. STAY is worse only if V < 3. Case 3: nobody else stays. STAY nets V-1; DROP nets +2. Again STAY is worse only if V < 3. Case 2 needs every rival to bid the minimum, and Case 3 needs every rival to drop, which they should not do (see below). So STAY weakly dominates DROP in practice. The dominance is only broken in the corner where you would win a sack worth under 3 at price 1. Expected sack value is well above 3. Each hand's cats sum to -8-5+3+5+8+11+15 = 29 over 9 cards, about 3.2 per card. With 4 players a 4-card sack averages about 12.9 before any Dog removal. So the only first-stage decision (step 6) is effectively always STAY. That makes the first reveal and the stay/drop poll near-empty steps. Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule: (a) 'Always DROP' earns +2 x 8 = 16, ending at 31 mice and 0 cat points. Every stayer who simply loses all auctions ends at 15 + 24 = 39 or more. Always-DROP loses to nearly any policy. (b) 'Always STAY, bid all mice' wins round 1 for 15 mice and a sack of about 13 minus the Dog effect, a net loss. It then sits at 0 mice, is forced to DROP, and is stuck on 2-mice bids. It loses. (c) 'Always STAY, bid 1' collects +3 per losing round, ending around 39. A sensible bidder who buys two sacks of value about 12 for about 6 each nets about +12 above the consolation path and beats it. So (c) can lose and is not a never-lose policy. Seats: the start player only breaks second-level ties, and the fewer-mice tie-break applies first, so there is no seat edge. No single bid amount is strictly dominant, but the STAY/DROP option is, so the check fails.

balanced.evidence:
Card pool per hand: cats -8-5+3+5+8+11+15 = 29, plus Rabbit 0 and Dog 0. One random card is removed, expected value 29/9 = 3.2, leaving about 25.8 per player over 8 placed cards. With 3 players, each holding a Dog 8/9 of the time, about 2.7 Dogs reach the sacks. A lone Dog removes the top cat, roughly 8 in a 3-card sack. Total cat value over the game is therefore about 77 - 21 = 56, or about 7 per sack.

The key decision is STAY or DROP. Relative to dropping (+2), a stayer is 3 mice worse at once (-1 fee), and the winner also pays the bid.

Payoff of STAY relative to DROP, with sack value V and winning bid b:
- Stay alone (b = 1): V - 4.
- Contested, you win: V - 3 - b.
- Contested, you lose: -3.
- Nobody stays: sack discarded.
For V = 7: alone gives +3; contested with b of about 3 gives the winner +1 and the loser -3. Staying pays when you have seeded a strong card and expect few rivals. It loses in blind bidding wars. No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does.

Thoughtless policies under the winner rule (highest total):
- Always DROP: a fixed 15 + 16 = 31 total with 0 cat points. It loses to a stayer who picks spots. Example: A seeds 15/11/8 and stays alone in 4 rounds on sacks worth about 8 each. A gains 4 x (8 - 4) = +16 over the drop baseline and finishes about 47 against 31. Always-drop is therefore not a never-lose policy. It does well only when the others burn value in bidding wars, which sensible players avoid.
- Always STAY and bid max: pays all mice each win. On a 7-point sack with 14 mice that is -8 relative. It loses to almost anyone.
- Always STAY and bid 1: outbid by any 2. It wins only when alone or on the fewer-mice tie-break. A sensible player who drops often holds more mice, but simply bids 2 and beats it. It is not dominant.
- Always place the first listed card (-8 first): this poisons the early sacks. The policy has to stay or drop as well, and either half is exploitable.

Seat order: simultaneous card placement, talk, stay and bids leave no informational edge. The start player only breaks the second-level tie, and it rotates. Each player's dealt hand differs only by the random removed card. Every player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Rules are complete:
- Same 9 cards each, minus 1 removed, gives 8 cards for exactly 8 rounds, so the last placement is forced.
- The minimum mice to stay (2) covers the fee plus the minimum bid, so mice never go negative.
- Winner ties are defined: fewer current mice (after the fee), then seat order from the start player.
- No-stayer and single-stayer cases are defined.
- Dog rule: exactly one Dog plus at least one cat removes the highest-valued cat. This is defined even if all cats are negative (the least negative is removed).
- The end condition and the total/tiebreak/draw rule are pure arithmetic on tracked numbers.

No board, judge or clock is needed. All simultaneous decisions are polls: placement, stay/drop and bid.

Limits: 15 steps <= 20; choice steps 4 <= 4 (place, talk, stay/drop, bid); 13 attributes <= 20; hidden elements 3 (hands, removed card, shuffled sack order) <= 3; 1 random draw per round (the shuffle; the removal is in setup); 8 rounds <= 40.

Talk is warranted and simultaneous. Players have opposed interests: each wants rivals to drop on good sacks and to buy poisoned ones. Claims about what one placed can be lies. Players can partly check claims against their own card, the revealed cards and the public discards. Following a rival's 'it is bad, drop' can cost you the sack.

This is not a cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply. The last round is still a live auction.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Sources of chance:
- The removed card shifts a hand's total from 14 (15 removed) to 37 (-8 removed). But cards go into shared sacks, so this changes your options more than your score.
- The shuffle decides which cards are seen before stay/bid. With 3 players, 1 of 3 cards is seen before stay and 2 of 3 before the bid.

What good play controls:
- Seeding a high cat in a round you mean to win.
- Dumping -8/-5 or the Dog in rounds you drop.
- Counting the public discards to infer the hidden cards: each player's remaining hand can be bounded from the discards and the removed-card uncertainty.
- Reading talk and rivals' mice to predict who stays.
- Sizing sealed bids against the fewer-mice tie-break.

Rough chance share of the result is about 25-35%. When all players play well, the winner is decided by placement timing and bid modelling, not the shuffle alone. A strong reasoner beats always-drop by about +16 in the worked example. The deal adds variety but can be overcome.
